title: Ephemeral Environments with Azure, Terraform & GitHub Actions
excerpt: How to build fully automated per‑PR ephemeral environments on Azure using Terraform, GitHub Actions, and containerized .NET + React apps.

body.raw:
# Introduction

An ephemeral environment is a short-lived, isolated deployment of an application. They are usually based on a branch or PR/MR. Ephemeral environments are spun up on-demand for running tests, previewing features, and collaborating asynchronously across teams.

This article describes the architecture, CI/CD workflows, and infrastructure structure used to implement ephemeral environments for a .NET + React application deployed on Azure using Terraform and GitHub Actions.

---

# Architecture Overview

<BlogImage
  src="/docs/Ephemeral Environment.drawio.png"
  alt="Ephemeral Environment Architecture"
  size="large"
/>

Each pull request targeting the `dev` branch triggers:

1. Creation of an isolated Azure environment  
2. Deployment of the application container images  
3. Cleanup once the PR is closed or merged  

### **Azure services used**

- **App Services**  
- **App Service Plan**  
- **Log Analytics Workspace**  
- **Application Insights**  
- **Azure Container Registry (ACR)**  
- **Azure Key Vault**  
- **Storage Account / Storage Container**

These components are provisioned via Terraform and parameterized based on PR numbers to ensure globally unique resource names.

<Prerequisites
  articles={[
    {
      title: "Terraform Backend Bootstrap using Azure OIDC",
      href: "/blog/backendtf",
      description: "Set up a secure backend using GitHub Actions and workload identity federation."
    }
  ]}
/>

---

# Infrastructure as Code (IaC)

Terraform is used to manage all Azure resources.

### Naming & configuration files

- **`locals.tf`** → Naming conventions  
- **`variables.tf`** → Location, tags, and environment (`dev`, `test`, `prod`, or PR ID)

### Landing zone assumption

The `dev`, `test`, and `prod` resource groups are assumed to already exist.  
These come from a **Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF)** landing zone:  
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/

### Terraform state

The state backend is stored in a dedicated `RG-Management` resource group:

- Storage Account  
- Containers per environment (including PR environments)

The following scripts configure state storage:

- `init-backend.yaml`  
- `bootstrap-backend.sh`

### Deployment behavior

- **Pull request → dev** → fully automated ephemeral environment creation  
- **Push → dev** → deploy to dev environment  
- **Test & prod** → manual workflow dispatch only  

This ensures production environments are controlled while PRs deploy automatically.

---

# CI/CD Pipeline

This solution uses **7 GitHub Actions workflows**, grouped into provisioning, deployment, and cleanup.

---

## 1. Bootstrap Terraform Backend (one-time)

Initializes Terraform state for `dev`, `test`, and `prod`.

Only the resource group must exist beforehand.

---

## 2. Terraform Plan & Apply

Triggered when Terraform files change or run manually.

Steps:

1. `terraform init`  
2. `terraform plan`  
3. `terraform apply`  

---

## 3. Container Build & Deploy

Triggered on changes to the `dev` branch or run manually.

Steps:

1. Docker build  
2. Read-only Terraform init  
3. Push image to ACR  
4. Deploy to App Services  

---

## 4. Terraform Destroy (manual cleanup)

Manually destroy infrastructure for a selected environment.

Steps:

1. `terraform init`  
2. `terraform plan`  
3. `terraform destroy`  

---

## 5. PR Terraform Plan & Apply (Ephemeral IaC)

Runs only for PRs targeting `dev`.

Steps:

1. `bootstrap-pr.sh` — sets up state container for PR  
2. `terraform init`  
3. `terraform plan`  
4. `terraform apply` with PR number as the environment name  

---

## 6. PR Container Build & Deploy (Ephemeral App)

Triggered after the ephemeral Terraform workflow completes.

Steps:

1. Build image from the triggering commit  
2. Terraform init (lookup deployed resources)  
3. Push to PR-specific ACR  
4. Deploy to ephemeral App Service  

---

## 7. Cleanup PR Terraform Backend

Triggered when the PR is closed or merged.

Steps:

1. `terraform init`  
2. `terraform plan`  
3. `terraform destroy`  

---

# Repository Structure

### `.github/Terraform/prod`
Terraform configuration for **dev**, **test**, and **prod** environments.

### `.github/Terraform/pr`
Terraform configuration for **ephemeral PR environments**.

Differences:

- Creates a **new resource group**  
- Assigns **AcrPull** role automatically to the App Service managed identity  

### `.github/workflow`
All GitHub Actions pipelines.

### `/reactapp.client`
React frontend.

### `/reactapp.Server`
.NET backend.

### `/docs`
Documentation images (used in this article).

---

# Deployment & Data Flow

## Ephemeral Environment Flow

<BlogImage
  src="/docs/Ephemeral Enviornments.jpg"
  alt="Ephemeral Environments Data Flow"
  size="large"
/>

1. Developer creates a feature branch  
2. PR opened against `dev`  
3. PR triggers IaC workflow  
4. Terraform provisions ephemeral environment  
5. Container workflow starts automatically  
6. Image built + deployed to ephemeral App Service  
7. Developer tests & validates  
8. PR merged/closed triggers destruction  
9. Environment removed automatically  

---

## Production Pipeline Flow

<BlogImage
  src="/docs/prod.jpg"
  alt="Production Pipeline"
  size="large"
/>

10. Change merged into `dev`  
11. *(Optional)* Terraform applies infra updates  
12. Docker image built & deployed to dev  
13. Manual PR from `dev` → `test`  
14. Manual workflow dispatch for test  
15. Manual PR from `test` → `main`  
16. Manual workflow dispatch for production  

---

# Troubleshooting

---

## “No available instances to satisfy this request”

<BlogImage
  src="/docs/error1.png"
  alt="App Service Capacity Error"
  size="medium"
/>

The region has temporarily exhausted App Service capacity.

**Fix:** Retry the job after ~10 minutes.

---

## Application Error

<BlogImage src="/docs/error2.png" alt="Application Error" size="medium" />

Check logs under:  
**App Service → Deployment Center → Logs**

Common issues:

- Missing `AcrPull` permissions  
- Incorrect Dockerfile  
- Failed container build  

---

## Resource Group Not Found

Verify:

- The resource group exists  
- The service principal has correct access scope  

---

## Federated Credentials Error

<BlogImage src="/docs/error3.png" alt="Federated Credentials Error" size="medium" />

Error: AADSTS700213: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion subject

Check:

- Branch, repo, and org names (case-sensitive!)  
- Environment exists  
- Federated credential configuration matches workflow

title: Terraform Backend Bootstrap using Azure OIDC & GitHub Actions
excerpt: Automating Azure Terraform backend creation using Service Principal, Federated Credentials, and GitHub Actions

body.raw:
# Terraform Backend Bootstrap using Azure OIDC & GitHub Actions

<BlogImage 
  src="/terraformazure.png" 
  alt="Terraform & Azure"
  size="large" 
/>

---

## What This Guide Covers

This guide focuses only on the **automatic backend bootstrap process**.

We will:

1. Create a Service Principal in Azure  
2. Configure Federated Credentials (OIDC)  
3. Assign required roles  
4. Store required IDs in GitHub  
5. Use GitHub Actions to create the Terraform backend 

---

## Architecture Overview

The goal is simple:

GitHub Actions → OIDC authentication → Azure → Create Storage Account + Container

No client secrets.  
No stored credentials.  
No manual backend provisioning.

---

# Phase 1 — Identity Setup in Azure

## Step 1 — Create a Service Principal

Create a Service Principal inside Azure.

You can follow the official Microsoft guide:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/howto-create-service-principal-portal

<BlogImage 
  src="/serviceacc.png" 
  alt="Create Service Principal"
  size="medium" 
/>

The Service Principal will act as the identity for GitHub Actions.

---

## Step 2 — Assign Required Role

The Service Principal needs permission to create:

- Resource Groups
- Storage Accounts
- Blob Containers

Assign:

**Contributor** role  
Scope: The subscription or specific resource group

<BlogImage 
  src="/roleassignment1.png" 
  alt="Create role assignment"
  size="medium" 
/>

<BlogImage 
  src="/contributor.png" 
  alt="Contributor role"
  size="medium" 
/>

Keep permissions scoped as narrowly as possible.

---

# Phase 2 — Configure Federated Credentials (OIDC)

Instead of using client secrets, we use **OIDC federation**.

This allows GitHub to authenticate securely without storing credentials.

## Step 3 — Add Federated Credential

Inside your Service Principal:

- Navigate to **Certificates & Secrets**
- Select **Federated Credentials**
- Add new credential

Choose:
- Scenario: GitHub Actions
- Organization
- Repository
- Branch (usually main)

<BlogImage 
  src="/fedcred1.png" 
  alt="Federated Credentials setup step 1"
  size="medium" 
/>

<BlogImage 
  src="/fedcred.png" 
  alt="Federated Credentials setup step 2"
  size="medium" 
/>

<BlogImage 
  src="/fedcred2.png" 
  alt="Federated Credentials setup step 3"
  size="medium" 
/>

<BlogImage 
  src="/fedcred3.png" 
  alt="Federated Credentials setup complete"
  size="medium" 
/>

This configuration allows GitHub to request an identity token that Azure trusts.

No secrets required.

---

# Phase 3 — Configure GitHub Repository Secrets

Although we are not storing passwords, GitHub still needs:

- Client ID  
- Tenant ID  
- Subscription ID  

These identify **where** authentication should happen.

Locate them in Azure:

<BlogImage 
  src="/tenantobjid.png" 
  alt="Tenant and Client ID"
  size="medium" 
/>

<BlogImage 
  src="/subid.png" 
  alt="Subscription ID"
  size="medium" 
/>

---

## Add Them to GitHub

In your repository:

Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret

Add:

- AZURE_CLIENT_ID
- AZURE_TENANT_ID
- AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID

<BlogImage 
  src="/secret1.png" 
  alt="GitHub secret setup step 1"
  size="medium" 
/>

<BlogImage 
  src="/secret2.png" 
  alt="GitHub secret setup step 2"
  size="medium" 
/>

These are identifiers — not passwords.

---

# Phase 4 — GitHub Workflow to Create Terraform Backend

This workflow creates:

- Resource Group  
- Storage Account  
- Blob Container  

It runs once to bootstrap the Terraform backend.

---

## backend.yaml

```yaml:title=.github/workflows/backend.yaml
name: BackendStorageCreate

on:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

env:
  location: "westeurope"
  terraformStorageRG: <resource-group-name>
  terraformStorageAccount: <storage-account-name>
  containerNameBackend: "tfstate"

jobs:
  setup-terraform-backend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Azure Login
        uses: azure/login@v2
        with:
          client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}

      - name: Create Backend Resources
        uses: azure/cli@v2
        with:
          azcliversion: latest
          inlineScript: |
            az group create \
              --name $terraformStorageRG \
              --location $location

            az storage account create \
              --name $terraformStorageAccount \
              --resource-group $terraformStorageRG \
              --location $location \
              --sku Standard_LRS

            az storage container create \
              --name $containerNameBackend \
              --account-name $terraformStorageAccount
```

# Sources Used
- [Terraform State Management: Understanding the Foundation of Infrastructure as Code](https://iamachs.com/blog/azure-terraform/part-4-state-management-basics)
- [How to store Terraform state file in Azure Storage](https://www.coachdevops.com/2022/03/how-to-store-terraform-state-file-in.html)

title: Manual Terraform Backend Setup in Azure
excerpt: Create an Azure Storage Account manually to store Terraform remote state

# Your content here

# Manual Terraform Backend Setup in Azure

<BlogImage 
  src="/azurestorage.png" 
  alt="Azure Storage Account for Terraform state"
  size="small" 
/>

---

## What This Guide Covers

This guide shows how to manually create the required Azure resources to store Terraform remote state.

We will create:

1. A Resource Group  
2. A Storage Account  
3. A Blob Container (tfstate)  

This is useful when:

- You want a quick local setup
- You are testing Terraform manually
- You are not yet using CI/CD automation
- You prefer understanding the resources before automating them

This guide does **not** cover GitHub Actions or OIDC authentication.

---

## Why Remote State?

Terraform state tracks all managed infrastructure.

Storing it locally:

- Prevents team collaboration  
- Risks accidental deletion  
- Causes state conflicts  

Using Azure Storage:

- Centralizes state  
- Enables state locking  
- Supports versioning  
- Improves reliability  

---

# Step 1 — Create a Resource Group

In the Azure Portal:

1. Navigate to **Resource Groups**
2. Select **Create**
3. Choose:
   - Subscription
   - Region
   - Name (example: terraform-backend-rg)

<BlogImage 
  src="/rg.png" 
  alt="Create Azure Resource Group"
  size="medium" 
/>

Click **Review + Create**, then **Create**.

---

# Step 2 — Create a Storage Account

Navigate to:

Storage Accounts → Create

Choose:

- Same Subscription  
- Resource Group created above  
- Unique Storage Account name  
- Region (same as resource group recommended)  
- Performance: Standard  
- Redundancy: LRS (sufficient for most cases)

<BlogImage 
  src="/strg.png" 
  alt="Create Azure Storage Account"
  size="medium" 
/>

Review and create.

---

## Storage Account Settings Recommendation

After creation:

- Enable **Blob versioning** (recommended)
- Keep public access disabled
- Use private networking unless required otherwise

<BlogImage 
  src="/strg2.png" 
  alt="Storage Account configuration"
  size="medium" 
/>

Blob versioning helps recover from accidental state corruption.

---

# Step 3 — Create the Backend Container

Inside your Storage Account:

1. Navigate to **Containers**
2. Click **+ Container**
3. Name it:
4. Access level: **Private**

<BlogImage 
  src="/strg3.png" 
  alt="Create Terraform state container"
  size="medium" 
/>

This container will store the terraform.tfstate

---

# Terraform Backend Configuration

Once the resources are created, configure Terraform to use them.

Add this block to your main.tf:

```hcl:title=main.tf
terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    resource_group_name  = "terraform-backend-rg"
    storage_account_name = "<yourstorageaccount>"
    container_name       = "tfstate"
    key                  = "terraform.tfstate"
  }
}
```

# Sources Used
- [Store Terraform state in Azure Storage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/terraform/store-state-in-azure-storage?tabs=azure-cli)

# How to Set Up a Markdown Blog Using Next.js, Tailwind CSS, and MDX This is how I built this website — a fully MDX‑powered blog running on the Next.js App Router.
--- # The Stack --- # Requirements & Installation You will need: - [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en) - Optionally: [nvm](https://www.nvmnode.com/) Create a new Next.js project: ``` pnpm create next-app@latest my-app --yes ``` Install Tailwind CSS: ``` pnpm install tailwindcss @tailwindcss/postcss postcss ``` And import it in your global stylesheet: ```css:title=global.css @import "tailwindcss"; ``` --- # Project strucure
This project uses the Next.js App Router, meaning routing is filesystem-based. Here's the simplified folder layout: ```bash └── project/ ├── app/ │ ├── blog/ │ │ ├── page.tsx │ │ ├── blog1/ │ │ │ └── blog1.mdx │ │ └── blog2/ │ │ └── blog2.mdx │ ├── page.tsx │ └── layout.tsx ├── tailwind.config.js ├── package.json ├── next.config.ts ├── mdx.d.ts ├── mdx-components.tsx └── components/ └── navbar.tsx ``` ### /App The app/ folder is the core of routing. - app/page.tsx → your homepage (/) - app/layout.tsx → shared layout (navigation, footers, wrappers) ### /App/Blog The blog system is completely filesystem-driven: - app/blog/page.tsx → /blog - Each subfolder → a blog post - blog1/blog1.mdx → /blog/blog1 - blog2/blog2.mdx → /blog/blog2 MDX files act like pages — no extra configuration needed once MDX is set up. ### /components Contains shared UI components such as a navigation bar. ### Other files - tailwind.config.ts - Tailwind CSS configuration - next.config.ts - Next.js configuration including MDX setup - package.json - dependencies and scripts - mdx.d.ts - MDX TypeScript support - mdx-components.tsx - overrides and custom components for MDX (links, images, code blocks, etc.) --- # MDX ## install mdx dependencies ``` pnpm add @next/mdx @mdx-js/loader @mdx-js/react @types/mdx ``` ## Configure next.config.tsx ```tsx:title=next.config.tsx import createMDX from '@next/mdx' import type { NextConfig } from 'next' const nextConfig = { pageExtensions: ['js', 'jsx', 'ts', 'tsx', 'md', 'mdx'], output: 'export', // Added for Azure static storage support } satisfies NextConfig export default createMDX({ extension: /\.(md|mdx)$/, })(nextConfig) ``` ## Add & Configure mdx-components.tsx ```tsx:title=mdx-components.tsx import type { MDXComponents } from 'mdx/types' const components: MDXComponents = {} export function useMDXComponents(): MDXComponents { return components } ``` ## Create a blog homepage & blog example Create a new folder under app called /blog and add a page.tsx. This solution links to the name of your blog folder. ### page.tsx ``` import Link from "next/link"; export default function BlogPage() { const blogs = [ { slug: "blog1", title: "Blog 1", description: "An introduction to the first blog post.", }, { slug: "blog2", title: "Blog 2", description: "A follow-up blog post with more details.", }, ]; return (

Blog

Welcome to the blog section. Here you'll find all published articles.

    {blogs.map((blog) => (

  • {blog.title}

    {blog.description}

    • ))}
); } ``` # Sources used:
- [Next.js Docs](https://nextjs.org/docs) - [Tailwindcss Docs](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/installation/framework-guides/nextjs) - [How to use markdown and MDX in Next.js](https://nextjs.org/docs/pages/guides/mdx) - [How I Built My Blog (original)](https://www.joshwcomeau.com/blog/how-i-built-my-blog/) - [How I Built My Blog](https://www.joshwcomeau.com/blog/how-i-built-my-blog-v2/) - [Guide to Writing MDX and Markdown](https://kabartolo.github.io/chicago-docs-demo/docs/mdx-guide/writing/)

title: Host a Static Website in Azure using Terraform, OIDC & GitHub Actions
excerpt: Fully automated static website hosting in Azure Storage using Terraform, GitHub Actions with OIDC authentication with custom domain hosting using Azure Front Door and Godaddy

body.raw:
# Host a Static Website in Azure Storage using Terraform, OIDC & GitHub Actions

This guide shows how to fully automate static website hosting in Azure using:

- Terraform
- Azure Storage (Static Website)
- GitHub Actions
- OIDC Authentication
- Azure Front Door
- Godaddy

This is a production-ready, GitOps-style deployment.

---

<Prerequisites
  articles={[
    {
      title: "Terraform Backend Bootstrap using Azure OIDC",
      href: "/blog/backendtf",
      description: "Provision the backend using GitHub Actions and federated identity."
    }
  ]}
/>

---

# Architecture Overview

GitHub Push  
→ GitHub Actions  
→ OIDC Authentication  
→ Terraform  
→ Azure Storage (Static Website)  
→ Azure Front Door  
→ Custom Domain  

State stored remotely in Azure.

---

# Step 1 — Storage Account with Static Website

Add the following to your Terraform configuration.

## strg.tf

```hcl:title=strg.tf
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "storage" {
  name                     = local.storage_name
  resource_group_name      = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name
  location                 = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "GRS"
}

resource "azurerm_storage_account_static_website" "static" {
  storage_account_id = azurerm_storage_account.storage.id
  index_document     = "index.html"
  error_404_document = "404.html"
}
```
After deployment, Azure automatically creates the $web container.

This container will host your static files.

--- 

# Step 2 — Azure Front Door

- Azure Front Door provides:
- Global routing
- HTTPS
- Custom domain support
- Edge acceleration

Custom domain is added manually later

###  frontdoor.tf

```hcl:title=strg.tf
resource "azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_profile" "frontDoor" {
  name                = local.frontdoor_name
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name
  sku_name            = "Standard_AzureFrontDoor"
}


resource "azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_endpoint" "endpoint" {
  name                     = "${local.frontdoor_name}-endpoint"
  cdn_frontdoor_profile_id = azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_profile.frontDoor.id
}

resource "azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin_group" "origin_group" {
  name                     = "${local.frontdoor_name}-origin-group"
  cdn_frontdoor_profile_id = azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_profile.frontDoor.id

  session_affinity_enabled = false

  load_balancing {
    sample_size                 = 4
    successful_samples_required = 3
  }

  health_probe {
    protocol = "Https"
    path     = "/"
    interval_in_seconds = 30
  }
}

locals {
  static_site_hostname = trimsuffix(
    replace(azurerm_storage_account.storageAccount.primary_web_endpoint, "https://", ""),
    "/"
  )
}


resource "azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin" "origin" {
  name                          = "${local.frontdoor_name}-origin"
  cdn_frontdoor_origin_group_id = azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin_group.origin_group.id

  host_name                    = local.static_site_hostname
  origin_host_header           = local.static_site_hostname
  certificate_name_check_enabled = true

  http_port  = 80
  https_port = 443
}


resource "azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_route" "route" {
  name                          = "${local.frontdoor_name}-route"
  cdn_frontdoor_endpoint_id     = azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_endpoint.endpoint.id
  cdn_frontdoor_origin_group_id = azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin_group.origin_group.id

  cdn_frontdoor_origin_ids = [
    azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin.origin.id
  ]

  supported_protocols = ["Http", "Https"]
  patterns_to_match   = ["/*"]

  forwarding_protocol     = "MatchRequest"
  https_redirect_enabled  = true
  link_to_default_domain  = true

  depends_on = [
    azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin_group.origin_group,
    azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin.origin,
    azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_endpoint.endpoint
  ]
}



```

# Step 3 — GitHub Actions Deployment Workflow

This workflow:
- Authenticates using OIDC
- Builds your static app
- Runs Terraform
- Uploads static content to $web

## deploy.yaml

```yaml:title=deploy.yaml
name: Deploy Static Website

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

env:
  ARM_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
  ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
  ARM_TENANT_ID: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "20"

      - name: Install & Build
        run: |
          npm install
          npm run build

      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v1

      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init -backend-config="use_oidc=true"

      - name: Terraform Apply
        run: terraform apply -auto-approve

      - name: Azure Login (OIDC)
        uses: azure/login@v1
        with:
          client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}

      - name: Upload Static Files
        uses: azure/CLI@v1
        with:
          inlineScript: |
            az storage blob upload-batch \
              --account-name <your-storage-account> \
              --source out \
              --destination '$web'
```

## Result

<BlogImage src="/frontdoor10.png" alt="FrontDoor" size="medium" />

# Step 4 — Custom Domain Configuration

You will need to add:

1. Domain
2. Configure/Associate Domain with endpoint & route

### Add a Domain

<BlogImage src="/frontdoor3.png" alt="Add custom domain" size="large" />
<BlogImage src="/frontdoor4.png" alt="Add custom domain" size="large" />

### Associate domain

<BlogImage src="/frontdoor9.png" alt="associate custom domain" size="large" />

Azure will provide:

- CNAME target
- TXT validation record
<BlogImage src="/frontdoor13.png" alt="Add custom domain" size="large" />

# Step 5 - Configure Godaddy

In GoDaddy DNS Management:

Add:

- CNAME → points to Front Door endpoint  
- TXT → validation value provided by Azure  

<BlogImage src="/godaddy.png" alt="GoDaddy DNS setup" size="medium" />
<BlogImage src="/godaddy2.png" alt="GoDaddy TXT setup" size="medium" />
<BlogImage src="/frontdoor12.png" alt="GoDaddy TXT setup" size="medium" />

Wait for DNS propagation.

# Final Result

<BlogImage src="/finalresult.png" alt="Final website result" size="large" />

`,(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.pre,{children:(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.code,{className:"language-hcl:title=strg.tf",children:`resource "azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_profile" "frontDoor" {\r
  name                = local.frontdoor_name\r
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name\r
  sku_name            = "Standard_AzureFrontDoor"\r
}\r
\r
\r
resource "azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_endpoint" "endpoint" {\r
  name                     = "\${local.frontdoor_name}-endpoint"\r
  cdn_frontdoor_profile_id = azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_profile.frontDoor.id\r
}\r
\r
resource "azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin_group" "origin_group" {\r
  name                     = "\${local.frontdoor_name}-origin-group"\r
  cdn_frontdoor_profile_id = azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_profile.frontDoor.id\r
\r
  session_affinity_enabled = false\r
\r
  load_balancing {\r
    sample_size                 = 4\r
    successful_samples_required = 3\r
  }\r
\r
  health_probe {\r
    protocol = "Https"\r
    path     = "/"\r
    interval_in_seconds = 30\r
  }\r
}\r
\r
locals {\r
  static_site_hostname = trimsuffix(\r
    replace(azurerm_storage_account.storageAccount.primary_web_endpoint, "https://", ""),\r
    "/"\r
  )\r
}\r
\r
\r
resource "azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin" "origin" {\r
  name                          = "\${local.frontdoor_name}-origin"\r
  cdn_frontdoor_origin_group_id = azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin_group.origin_group.id\r
\r
  host_name                    = local.static_site_hostname\r
  origin_host_header           = local.static_site_hostname\r
  certificate_name_check_enabled = true\r
\r
  http_port  = 80\r
  https_port = 443\r
}\r
\r
\r
resource "azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_route" "route" {\r
  name                          = "\${local.frontdoor_name}-route"\r
  cdn_frontdoor_endpoint_id     = azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_endpoint.endpoint.id\r
  cdn_frontdoor_origin_group_id = azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin_group.origin_group.id\r
\r
  cdn_frontdoor_origin_ids = [\r
    azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin.origin.id\r
  ]\r
\r
  supported_protocols = ["Http", "Https"]\r
  patterns_to_match   = ["/*"]\r
\r
  forwarding_protocol     = "MatchRequest"\r
  https_redirect_enabled  = true\r
  link_to_default_domain  = true\r
\r
  depends_on = [\r
    azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin_group.origin_group,\r
    azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_origin.origin,\r
    azurerm_cdn_frontdoor_endpoint.endpoint\r
  ]\r
}\r
\r
\r

`,(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.pre,{children:(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.code,{className:"language-yaml:title=deploy.yaml",children:`name: Deploy Static Website\r
\r
on:\r
  push:\r
    branches:\r
      - main\r
\r
permissions:\r
  id-token: write\r
  contents: read\r
\r
env:\r
  ARM_CLIENT_ID: \${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}\r
  ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID: \${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}\r
  ARM_TENANT_ID: \${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}\r
\r
jobs:\r
  deploy:\r
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\r
\r
    steps:\r
      - name: Checkout\r
        uses: actions/checkout@v4\r
\r
      - name: Setup Node\r
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4\r
        with:\r
          node-version: "20"\r
\r
      - name: Install & Build\r
        run: |\r
          npm install\r
          npm run build\r
\r
      - name: Setup Terraform\r
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v1\r
\r
      - name: Terraform Init\r
        run: terraform init -backend-config="use_oidc=true"\r
\r
      - name: Terraform Apply\r
        run: terraform apply -auto-approve\r
\r
      - name: Azure Login (OIDC)\r
        uses: azure/login@v1\r
        with:\r
          client-id: \${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}\r
          tenant-id: \${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}\r
          subscription-id: \${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}\r
\r
      - name: Upload Static Files\r
        uses: azure/CLI@v1\r
        with:\r
          inlineScript: |\r
            az storage blob upload-batch \\\r
              --account-name <your-storage-account> \\\r

title: Host a Static Website in Azure (Manual Portal Setup)
excerpt: Step-by-step manual guide to hosting a static website in Azure Storage and exposing it securely using Azure Front Door with a custom domain.

body.raw:
# Host a Static Website in Azure (Manual Portal Setup)

This guide walks through hosting a static website entirely through the Azure Portal — no Terraform, no automation.

You will:

- Create a Storage Account  
- Enable Static Website hosting  
- Deploy your site files  
- Configure Azure Front Door  
- Connect a custom domain (GoDaddy example)

---

# Part 1 — Azure Storage Static Website

## 1. Create a Resource Group

Start by creating a new Resource Group.

<BlogImage src="/rg.png" alt="Create Resource Group" size="medium" />

Choose:
- Subscription
- Region
- Logical name (e.g. rg-static-website)

---

## 2. Create a Storage Account

Navigate to **Storage Accounts → Create**

<BlogImage src="/strg.png" alt="Create Storage Account" size="medium" />
<BlogImage src="/strg2.png" alt="Storage configuration" size="medium" />

Recommended settings:

- Performance: Standard
- Redundancy: GRS (or LRS for dev/test)
- Networking: Public endpoint enabled

---

## 3. Enable Static Website Hosting

Inside the Storage Account:

Data Management → Static Website → Enable

<BlogImage src="/statstrg.png" alt="Enable static website" size="medium" />

Configure:

- Index document name → index.html
- Error document → 404.html

Azure automatically creates a special container called: $web


This is where your static files must live.

---

# Part 2 — Deploy Your Static Site

After building your site locally:

```
pnpm build
```


(or npm run build depending on your project)

You now have a static output folder (commonly /out or /build).

---

## Option 1 — Upload via Azure Portal

Go to:

Storage Account → Containers → $web → Upload

<BlogImage src="/deploy.png" alt="Upload to web container" size="small" />

Upload the contents of your build folder.

Once complete, open:

Static Website → Primary Endpoint

You should now see your site live.

<BlogImage src="/result.png" alt="Static website result" size="large" />

---

# Part 3 — Add Azure Front Door (Global HTTPS + CDN)

Azure Storage endpoints are public but not optimized for:

- Global performance  
- Automatic HTTPS certificates  
- Custom domain routing  

Azure Front Door solves this.

---

## 1. Create Azure Front Door

Search for **Front Door and CDN profiles** → Create

<BlogImage src="/frontdoor1.png" alt="Create Front Door" size="large" />
<BlogImage src="/frontdoor2.png" alt="Front Door configuration" size="small" />

Choose:

- SKU: Standard Azure Front Door
- Resource Group: same as storage


---

## 2. Configure Route

Create a route linking:

Frontend endpoint → Origin group

<BlogImage src="/frontdoor8.png" alt="Domain validation" size="medium" />

Enable:

- HTTPS redirect
- HTTP → HTTPS enforcement

---

## 3. Verify Default Endpoint

After deployment, open the default Front Door domain.

<BlogImage src="/frontdoor10.png" alt="Front Door result" size="large" />

Your static site should now load globally via Front Door.

---

# Part 4 — Connect a Custom Domain (GoDaddy Example)

To use your own domain:

- Add a CNAME record
- Validate ownership via TXT record

---

## 1. Add Custom Domain in Front Door

Go to:

Front Door → Domains
<BlogImage src="/frontdoor3.png" alt="Add custom domain" size="large" />
<BlogImage src="/frontdoor4.png" alt="Add custom domain" size="large" />
<BlogImage src="/frontdoor9.png" alt="Add custom domain" size="large" />
<BlogImage src="/frontdoor11.png" alt="Add custom domain" size="large" />



Azure will provide:

- CNAME target
- TXT validation record
<BlogImage src="/frontdoor13.png" alt="Add custom domain" size="large" />
---

## 2. Configure DNS in GoDaddy

In GoDaddy DNS Management:

Add:

- CNAME → points to Front Door endpoint  
- TXT → validation value provided by Azure  

<BlogImage src="/godaddy.png" alt="GoDaddy DNS setup" size="medium" />
<BlogImage src="/godaddy2.png" alt="GoDaddy TXT setup" size="medium" />
<BlogImage src="/frontdoor12.png" alt="GoDaddy TXT setup" size="medium" />

Wait for DNS propagation.

---

# Final Result

You now have:

- Static site hosted in Azure Storage  
- Global acceleration via Azure Front Door  
- Automatic HTTPS  
- Custom domain connected  

<BlogImage src="/finalresult.png" alt="Final website result" size="large" />

---

# When Should You Use This Manual Approach?

Use this when:

- Learning Azure fundamentals
- Deploying a quick personal site
- Testing architecture before automation
- Avoiding infrastructure-as-code complexity

If you plan to manage multiple environments or production workloads, automation is strongly recommended.

---

title: Deploying Terraform to Azure using GitHub Actions (OIDC)
excerpt: Run Terraform init, plan and apply in GitHub Actions using Azure OIDC authentication

# Deploying Terraform to Azure using GitHub Actions (OIDC)

<BlogImage 
  src="/terraformazure.png" 
  alt="Terraform & GitHub Actions"
  size="large" 
/>

---

## What This Guide Covers

This article assumes that Backend storage exists for storing state

<Prerequisites
  articles={[
    {
      title: "Manual Terraform Backend Setup in Azure",
      href: "/blog/backendportal",
      description: "Create the Azure Storage Account manually via the Azure Portal."
    },
    {
      title: "Terraform Backend Bootstrap using Azure OIDC",
      href: "/blog/backendtf",
      description: "Provision the backend using GitHub Actions and federated identity."
    }
  ]}
/>

It also assumes:

- OIDC authentication between GitHub and Azure is configured
- Required repository secrets are stored

If not, complete the backend and identity setup first.

This guide focuses purely on:

→ Running Terraform from GitHub Actions  
→ Using OIDC authentication  
→ Connecting to a remote Azure backend  

---

# Deployment Architecture

GitHub Actions  
→ OIDC Authentication  
→ Azure  
→ Remote Backend (Storage Account)  
→ Infrastructure Deployment  

No local execution required.  
No stored credentials.

---

# Minimal Terraform Configuration

Below is a simple Terraform setup using the AzureRM provider and OIDC authentication.

## main.tf

```hcl:title=main.tf
terraform {
  required_providers {
    azurerm = {
      source = "hashicorp/azurerm"
      version = "~> 4.61.0"
    }
  }
backend "azurerm" {}
}


provider "azurerm" {
   features {}
   use_oidc = true
}

# Resource Group
resource "azurerm_resource_group" "rg" {
  name     = local.rg_name
  location = var.location
}
```
## variables.tf
```hcl:title=variables.tf
variable "location" {
  type    = string
  default = "westeurope"
}
```

## locals.tf
```hcl:title=locals.tf
locals {
  base    = "simpletst"
  rg_name = "${local.base}-rg"
}
```

This keeps the infrastructure example intentionally simple.

# GitHub Actions Workflow

This workflow:
- Authenticates using OIDC
- Initializes Terraform with remote backend
- Validates and formats code
- Runs plan
- Applies automatically on main

## terraform.yaml
```yaml:title=terraform.yaml
name: Terraform Plan & Apply

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths:
      - ".github/Terraform/**"
      - ".github/workflows/terraform.yaml"
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

env:
  ARM_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
  ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
  ARM_TENANT_ID: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}

  RESOURCE_GROUP: <backend-resource-group>
  STORAGE_ACCOUNT: <backend-storage-account>
  location: westeurope

jobs:
  terraform:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: .github/Terraform
        shell: bash

    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v1

      - name: Terraform Init
        run: |
          terraform init \
            -backend-config="resource_group_name=$RESOURCE_GROUP" \
            -backend-config="storage_account_name=$STORAGE_ACCOUNT" \
            -backend-config="container_name=tfstate" \
            -backend-config="key=terraform.tfstate" \
            -backend-config="use_oidc=true"

      - name: Terraform Format
        run: terraform fmt -recursive

      - name: Terraform Validate
        run: terraform validate

      - name: Terraform Plan
        run: terraform plan -input=false -var location=$location

      - name: Terraform Apply
        run: terraform apply -auto-approve -input=false -var location=$location
```

## How It Works

1. GitHub requests an OIDC token
2. Azure validates it via federated identity
3. Terraform initializes using the remote backend
4. Plan and apply execute inside the runner
5. State is written to Azure Storage

### This ensures:

- No local state
- No client secrets
- Reproducible deployments
- Fully automated infrastructure changes

# Deployment Flow

Push to main

→ GitHub workflow triggers

→ Terraform runs

→ Azure resources update

→ Remote state updated

Infrastructure becomes Git-driven.


# Result

You now have:

- Remote Terraform state
- OIDC-based authentication
- CI/CD infrastructure deployment
- Zero local dependency

This completes the GitOps-style workflow.

# Sources used

- [How to Use Terraform in GitHub Actions](https://www.env0.com/blog/terraform-github-actions)
- [Deploy to Azure infrastructure with GitHub Actions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/devops/deliver/iac-github-actions)

`,(0,t.jsxDEV)(e.pre,{children:(0,t.jsxDEV)(e.code,{className:"language-yaml:title=terraform.yaml",children:`name: Terraform Plan & Apply\r
\r
on:\r
  push:\r
    branches:\r
      - main\r
    paths:\r
      - ".github/Terraform/**"\r
      - ".github/workflows/terraform.yaml"\r
  workflow_dispatch:\r
\r
permissions:\r
  id-token: write\r
  contents: read\r
\r
env:\r
  ARM_CLIENT_ID: \${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}\r
  ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID: \${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}\r
  ARM_TENANT_ID: \${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}\r
\r
  RESOURCE_GROUP: <backend-resource-group>\r
  STORAGE_ACCOUNT: <backend-storage-account>\r
  location: westeurope\r
\r
jobs:\r
  terraform:\r
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\r
\r
    defaults:\r
      run:\r
        working-directory: .github/Terraform\r
        shell: bash\r
\r
    steps:\r
      - name: Checkout\r
        uses: actions/checkout@v3\r
\r
      - name: Setup Terraform\r
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v1\r
\r
      - name: Terraform Init\r
        run: |\r
          terraform init \\\r
            -backend-config="resource_group_name=$RESOURCE_GROUP" \\\r
            -backend-config="storage_account_name=$STORAGE_ACCOUNT" \\\r
            -backend-config="container_name=tfstate" \\\r
            -backend-config="key=terraform.tfstate" \\\r
            -backend-config="use_oidc=true"\r
\r
      - name: Terraform Format\r
        run: terraform fmt -recursive\r
\r
      - name: Terraform Validate\r
        run: terraform validate\r
\r
      - name: Terraform Plan\r
        run: terraform plan -input=false -var location=$location\r
\r
      - name: Terraform Apply\r
        run: terraform apply -auto-approve -input=false -var location=$location
